What Diagnosis Is Supposed To Be

  Per the design doc, diagnosis is the step after Phase 0 for strategies with PF > 1.0.

  The intended flow in docs/autoresearch-pipeline-v7.md is:

  1. Take the enriched Phase 0 trade log.
  2. Slice it across all predefined dimensions.
  3. Rank which dimensions look like “capital leaks”.
  4. Summarize continuous values separately.
  5. Optionally include exit re-simulation results.
  6. Feed all of that into the hypothesis generator.
  7. Backtest 3 candidate fixes.
  8. Lock the winner and repeat next round.

  So diagnosis is not a backtest. It is a ranking and interpretation stage.

  What The Matrix Actually Computes

  The core function is compute_diagnosis_matrix(...) in src/backtesting/autoresearch/renko/diagnosis/matrix.py.

  It has a fixed _DIMENSIONS table. Each row defines:

  - dimension
  - source column
  - layer
  - category
  - mapped toggle

  That means diagnosis is not free-form. It only evaluates the dimensions hardcoded in _DIMENSIONS.

  For each dimension, _bad_mask(...) defines which rows are considered “bad”. Examples:

  - stock_rs_direction == -1 for long trades
  - mtf_score < 2
  - ema40_position == "below" for long trades
  - brick_zone_sign == "negative" for long trades
  - stop_distance_bricks > 5
  - prior_extension_negated == True

  Then compute_diagnosis_matrix(...) does:

  - baseline_pf = PF(all rows)
  - for each dimension:
      - remove the bad subgroup
      - recompute PF on the kept rows
      - proxy_pf_impact = proxy_pf - baseline_pf
      - capital_saved_pct = losses in bad subgroup / total losses
  - sort descending by proxy_pf_impact
  - return a src/backtesting/autoresearch/renko/models.py:136

  So the ranked table is a pure arithmetic ranking on the trade log. No backtest is run here.

  What The Continuous Summary Computes

  The continuous part is in src/backtesting/autoresearch/renko/diagnosis/continuous.py.

  It splits rows into:

  - winners: PnL > 0

• Findings

  - [P1] Shared S3 diagnosis prefixes can contaminate a fresh run with stale prior-run rounds. The orchestrator reads and writes every strate
    gy under a stable prefix, s3://.../diagnosis/$strat/round_N, with no run identifier and no cleanup before starting, then chooses “latest”
    from whatever is already there. If an earlier run left higher-numbered rounds behind, a restarted or clean-state run can download old dia
    gnosis.json / results.json and continue from the wrong point. This is separate from the lexicographic bug: even with numeric sorting fixe
    d, the script still assumes the prefix contains only the current run’s artifacts. See scripts/local_orchestrate_diagnosis.sh:115, scripts
    /local_orchestrate_diagnosis.sh:187, and scripts/local_orchestrate_diagnosis.sh:190.
  - [P1] Preserve prior-round context in the hypothesis prompt. From round 2 onward, the local orchestrator passes empty hypothesis_log and
    strategy_cards, unlike the in-repo diagnosis loop. That drops the list of already locked toggles and prior failed lessons from the prompt,
    so the model can reasonably re-propose a locked toggle or ignore prior-round learnings. See scripts/local_orchestrate_diagnosis.sh:157
    versus src/backtesting/autoresearch/renko/diagnosis/loop.py:106.
  - [P2] Pick the latest round numerically, not by the last S3 listing entry. latest_round_for_strategy() just remembers the final aws s3 ls
    prefix it sees. Once round_10 exists, lexicographic ordering can make round_9 appear later, so the orchestrator resumes from stale
    artifacts. See scripts/local_orchestrate_diagnosis.sh:190.
  - [P2] run_remote_stage() can spin forever after a successful command if the done marker is missing from StandardOutputContent. The helper
    only returns on Success when grep finds the marker; otherwise it keeps polling forever because Success is not treated as terminal without
    the marker. That assumes SSM always returns the full stdout and that the marker is never truncated out of the response. These commands
    pipe noisy Python output through tee, so a long enough run can hit SSM output truncation and hang the orchestrator even though the remote
    step already succeeded. See scripts/local_orchestrate_diagnosis.sh:91.
  - [P2] Avoid failing the backup when no /tmp artifacts exist. The find ... -print0 | tar --files-from - pipeline hands tar an empty list on
    clean instances, and tar exits non-zero. With set -euo pipefail, that aborts the entire backup after the main repo/data/cache uploads
    already succeeded. See aws/backup-instance-to-s3.sh:30.
  - [P3] The orchestrator no longer “discovers all Phase 0 edge keys from EC2 state”; it runs a hardcoded strategy list. If the survivor set
    changes, new edge strategies are silently skipped and removed/non-edge strategies are still attempted. That is an operational assumption
    baked into the script, and it directly contradicts the script header. See scripts/local_orchestrate_diagnosis.sh:3 and scripts/

what do you think of this feedback to mechanism path

 The mechanism path is the right path. But it has one structural flaw.

  The hypothesis pipeline is a smart toggle picker. It's useful but limited — it can only select from existing filters. It will never discover
   anything new. It's an optimization algorithm wearing an LLM costume.

  The mechanism pipeline is genuinely different. It asks the LLM to reason about why trades fail structurally — choppy corrections, exhausted
  impulses, no runway. That's real edge discovery. The prompt design is good: it explicitly says "prefer structural explanations over
  gate-selection stories" and "do not propose simple parameter tuning." You've thought carefully about this.

  The structural flaw: the pipeline asks the LLM for structural reasoning but then forces the output into {"feature":
  "correction_depth_ratio", "op": ">=", "value": 1.15}. The moment you do that, the LLM's edge discovery gets compressed into a parameter. The
   mechanism ("choppy corrections fail") is the edge. The threshold (choppiness_ratio <= 0.4) is just one possible encoding, and it's fragile.

  What I'd change — and it's not much

  1. Split the output into two stages.

  Stage 1 (LLM): produce the mechanism hypothesis — the qualitative structural insight. This is what you already get in failure_mechanism and
  evidence fields. That's the valuable part.

  Stage 2 (separate, non-LLM): translate that mechanism into a testable rule. This could be the LLM again, or it could be you manually, or a
  simpler code generator. The point is: the discovery step and the encoding step should be decoupled so the LLM isn't incentivized to dumb
  down its reasoning to fit a JSON schema.

  Right now build_mechanism_hypotheses.py does both in one shot. The LLM simultaneously discovers and encodes. That biases it toward
  mechanisms it can easily express as numeric comparisons.

  2. Show the LLM actual trades, not just summaries.

  This is the biggest improvement you can make. Your prompt gives the LLM winner_avg=3.2, loser_avg=4.1 style summaries. But LLMs reason much
  better from concrete examples. Show it 5 specific winning trades and 5 specific losing trades with their full brick sequence context — the
  impulse, the pullback shape, the entry point, what happened after. Let it pattern-match across examples. That's where LLMs genuinely
  discover things humans miss.

  3. Let the LLM ask for more data.

  Right now it's a single-shot prompt → response. The best mechanism discoveries will come from a multi-turn dialogue: LLM sees trades → forms
   initial hypothesis → asks "show me all losers where the impulse was < 5 bricks" → refines → asks "now show me winners with the same impulse
   size" → realizes the real distinguisher isn't impulse size but something else. That iterative narrowing is how real research works.

  4. Don't hardcode the feature set.

  full_mechanism_pipeline.py extracts 18 specific features. If the LLM discovers a mechanism that doesn't map to those 18 features — say "the
  breakout bar was a gap-up that got immediately filled" — it can't express it. The feature extraction should be extensible based on what
  mechanisms the LLM discovers, not fixed upfront.

  What NOT to change

  - Keep it in tmp/ as a research sidecar. Don't merge it into the production hypothesis loop yet.
  - Keep the trade-log replay validation. Even approximate PF estimates are better than trusting the LLM's confidence.
  - Keep the Shah grounding in the prompt. That's a real moat — it constrains the LLM to market-structure reasoning rather than statistical
  artifacts.
  - The rule_shape taxonomy (composite_filter, sequence_rule, state_transition, entry_veto) is good. Mechanisms really do fall into these
  categories.

do you agree with this feedback

 Architecture (Good)

  The pipeline implements exactly the two-stage split I suggested:

  context_extraction → examples_extraction → discovery (qualitative) → encoding (rules) → manifest

  This is the right architecture. Discovery is decoupled from encoding. The examples extractor gives the LLM actual brick sequences. The
  prompt explicitly says "do not encode rules as numeric thresholds yet." All good.

  ---
  The Critical Problem: Default Mode Is a Template, Not Discovery

  Both build_mechanism_discovery_v2.py and build_mechanism_encoding_v2.py default to hardcoded local functions when SIDECAR2_USE_MODEL is
  unset (which is the EC2 default).

  _local_discoveries() (line 152-242) always returns the same 3 mechanisms:
  - continuation_runway_too_small
  - correction_is_chop_not_pause
  - regime_alignment_is_insufficient

  The mechanism IDs, failure descriptions, structural signatures, and encoding guidance are static strings. The only dynamic parts are the
  evidence fields, which paste in computed stats (flip rates, stop distances). But the conclusions are predetermined.

  _local_encodings() (line 125-243) uses a dict lookup keyed on those exact 3 mechanism IDs. Same thresholds every time:
  correction_depth_ratio >= 1.15, trend_age_bricks <= 16, correction_choppiness_ratio <= 0.45, etc.

  This means: you built a 5-stage pipeline with full EC2 observability, S3 progress sync, preflight checks, and time auditing — that in
  default mode extracts rich data, throws it away, and returns hardcoded templates. The entire examples extraction step (loading brick caches,
   stratified sampling, building brick contexts) is wasted work when the discovery step ignores it.

  I understand why — you want EC2 to run without model dependency. But the result is a prototype that looks like it works but isn't actually
  doing discovery. It's running the plumbing without turning on the water.

  ---
  Orchestrator Runs Discovery/Encoding Twice

  In run_mechanism_sidecar2.py, both discovery and encoding are called twice:

  1. First with --prompt-out (writes prompt, returns immediately)
  2. Then again without it (actually generates output)

  Each invocation re-loads all the JSON inputs. In the EC2 shell runner (run_mechanism_sidecar2_ec2.sh), this is also visible —
  discovery_prompt_build and discovery_build are separate run_stage calls that both invoke the same script with different args. The script
  should accept --prompt-out alongside normal execution so it writes the prompt AND generates output in one pass.

  ---
  No Backtest Validation Step

  Sidecar1's full_mechanism_pipeline.py had evaluate_mechanism_rules() — it compiled the rules, filtered the trade log, and computed PF
  deltas. Sidecar2 stops at manifest generation. The manifest has conditions, required_features, and validation_checks — but nothing executes
  those checks.

  The pipeline produces a test plan but never runs the test. You'd need to manually feed the manifest into full_mechanism_pipeline.py or write
   a new evaluation step.

  ---
  Specific Code Issues

  1. Discovery evidence uses data but conclusions don't. _local_discoveries computes loser_flip, winner_flip, loser_stop, winner_stop — then
  hardcodes the conclusion regardless. If winners had HIGHER flip rates than losers, the function would still claim "losers show immediate
  mixed/reversing bricks." The evidence might contradict the mechanism.

  2. Encoding template mismatch risk. If you run discovery with model (SIDECAR2_USE_MODEL=1) but encoding without, the model might return
  mechanism IDs like "exhausted_impulse" that don't match the hardcoded template dict. Result: all 3 mechanisms get "encoding_status":
  "needs_more_examples" with empty encodings.

  3. _select_examples can oversample. Line 111: head(per_bucket * len(buckets)) — with per_bucket=5 and 4 loser exit-reason buckets, this
  returns up to 20 losers. Combined with per-bucket sampling of max(1, per_bucket // 2) + 1 median = 3-4 per bucket, the actual count varies
  unpredictably. Not a bug, but the example count fed to the LLM isn't controlled.

  4. _brick_context uses argmin on absolute nanosecond deltas. Line 125: deltas = np.abs((brick_index - ts).asi8). If the entry timestamp
  doesn't match any brick closely (e.g., different timezone convention, or the 05:00 index bug you've seen before), it silently matches the
  nearest brick which could be days away. No tolerance check — it always matches something.

  5. repair_sidecar2_staged_diagnosis.py hardcodes paths. Line 19: stage_root = Path("/tmp/sidecar2_new") and line 20: strategy_label =
  "renko-123-pullback@0.0100". Should be CLI args.

  6. EC2 runner's baseline contract check uses exit code 2 for mismatch (line 210 in the inline Python), which triggers fail_stage. This is
  correct behavior but the error message could be more specific — it says "baseline contract mismatch" without printing which fields diverged
  to the stage log (the details go to stdout which gets captured, not to the error message).

  ---
  What's Actually Good

  - The EC2 shell runner is excellent. Stage-by-stage timing, progress JSON with S3 sync, preflight validation, stdout/stderr capture,
  artifact collection. This is production-grade observability for a research pipeline.
  - The examples extractor is well-designed. Stratified sampling by exit reason, top PnL + median for diversity, actual brick sequences with
  configurable pre/post windows, all book fields included. This is exactly the right data to show an LLM.
  - The prompt design is sound. Ranked diagnosis clues (top 12 only — not overwhelming), trade-log summary, concrete examples with brick
  context, prior round results, and explicit instructions to stay qualitative. The asks_for_more_data field in the output schema is a good
  signal for iterative refinement.
  - The encoding feature library is well-organized by category (universe, trend, momentum, volatility, risk_extension). This gives the LLM
  clear scope for what's expressible.
  - The baseline contract check catches the diagnosis-vs-phase0 drift bug that Codex flagged.

  ---
  What I'd Do

  1. Make model mode the real path, not the afterthought. The whole point of sidecar2 is LLM discovery. The local fallback should be clearly
  labeled as "stub for testing the plumbing" not "default mode." On EC2, either set SIDECAR2_USE_MODEL=1 or don't run it at all.
  2. Add a validation/evaluation stage. After manifest, compile the rules and replay against the enriched trade log — same as
  full_mechanism_pipeline.py does. The pipeline should end with PF delta numbers, not a JSON plan.
  3. Add a tolerance check to brick matching. If the nearest brick is > 2 days from the entry timestamp, mark matched: false instead of
  silently matching garbage.
  4. Merge prompt generation into the main run. Pass --prompt-out alongside normal execution so each script runs once, not twice.
  5. Make the local fallback data-driven. If you must have a no-model path, at least make it conditional: look at actual flip rates, stop
  distances, and exit mixes to decide which of the 3 mechanisms has evidence and skip the ones that don't. Right now it asserts all 3
  regardless of data.

   filters return 0 entries. When _pre_filter_signals tries to join indicator values (at 05:00) with signal dates (at 00:00 from daily OHLCV),
   the reindex produces all NaN. The gate logic sees NaN → treats as "does not pass" → filters out every signal → 0 trades.

  timestamp. If these are off by 1 bar (which is likely — the brick forms during the day, the signal fires on the daily close), the mask is
  True on date X while the signal is True on date X+1. No overlap → 0 trades.

  - build_mechanism_test_manifest.py — convert hypotheses to implementation-oriented manifest
  - full_mechanism_pipeline.py — extract 18 structural features from detector, compile JSON rules, replay against trade log
  - backtest_mechanism_rules.py — simple trade-log replay with 3 hardcoded boolean-column rules

  Real-engine validation:
  - run_temp_mechanism_backtest.py — run mechanisms through actual signal engine + backtest
  - renko123_current_mechanism_refine.py — parameter sweep on runway_min/corr_min
  - renko123_orderly_mechanism_engine.py — real engine test: correction_depth + runway + zero reversals
  - renko123_orderly_mechanism_refine.py — parameter sweep on runway/corr/max_reversals
  - renko123_maturity_mechanism_engine.py — real engine test: correction_depth + runway + breakout_maturity <= 10
  - renko123_mechanism_qualifier_sweep.py — cross 3 mechanisms × 20 qualifier gates, run all 60 combos

  Rule definitions: v3, v4, v5_orderly, v6_maturity JSON files

  ---
  What's good

  1. The overall research progression is sound. Trade-log replay (fast, approximate) → real-engine validation (slow, accurate) → parameter
  refinement → qualifier sweep. This is the right order for mechanism research.

  2. backtest_mechanism_rules.py is clean and correct. Frozen dataclasses, clear separation of rule spec from evaluation, proper PF/win-rate
  computation, comparison against both baseline and toggle-loop best. The 3 rules (shallow_noise, structured_continuation,
  structured_plus_momentum) are layered correctly — each adds one more condition to the prior.

  3. build_mechanism_hypotheses.py prompt design is thoughtful. Lines 318-319: "Use them as clues about failure mechanisms, not as
  instructions to pick gates." Line 355: "Prefer structural explanations over gate-selection stories." Lines 360-361: "Do not propose simple
  parameter tuning, brute-force search, or generic gate stacking." These instructions steer the LLM toward genuine mechanism discovery.

  4. renko123_mechanism_qualifier_sweep.py is the most sophisticated real-engine script. It crosses 3 mechanism filters × 20 qualifier gates =
   60 combinations, with a trade floor check (>= 300 trades). The prior_ext_negated_filter is handled as a post-backtest filter on trade
  records rather than a pre-signal gate, which is the correct approach since extension negation is only known after the trade completes.

  5. EC2 runner runs full_mechanism_pipeline and run_temp_mechanism_backtest in parallel (lines 72-90), which is efficient since they're
  independent.

  ---
  What's well-designed

  1. Clean separation of concerns. Each module does one thing. matrix.py is pure functions (no I/O). continuous.py is pure functions.
  positions.py handles schema normalization. runner.py handles LLM + parallel backtest. No module reaches into another's internals.

  2. Data contracts are solid. models.py uses frozen dataclasses consistently. RenkoAutoresearchState is the only mutable container —
  everything it holds is immutable. This is the correct pattern for safe concurrent access.

  3. The diagnosis matrix is direction-aware throughout. Every _bad_mask in matrix.py checks direction == "long" vs "short" before applying
  the filter. Long trades check for bullish indicators, short trades check for bearish equivalents. This is critical for correctness and is
  done consistently across all 22 dimensions.

  4. Convergence logic is principled. 3 consecutive rounds below 0.05 PF improvement → stop. Safety cap at 20 rounds. Only toggles with >=
  threshold improvement get locked. Low-impact winners are tracked but not locked (lines 164-170 in loop.py).

  5. Cross-strategy learning via strategy cards. pipeline.py:243-245 feeds completed strategy cards into subsequent strategies' Opus prompts.
  card.py extracts both locked toggles (what worked) and lessons from LOST hypotheses (what proxy-real divergence teaches). This is a genuine
  moat — later strategies learn from earlier ones.

  6. LLM fallback chain. Opus → Codex gpt-5.4 via local Responses API → Codex CLI. Three layers of fallback with proper error handling.
  codex_runner.py handles JSONL parsing, timeout cleanup, and process lifecycle correctly.

  7. backtest_factory.py handles derived indicators gracefully. When the indicator cache doesn't contain pre-computed columns (like
  ema40_bounce_state), it computes them on-the-fly from raw indicators (lines 196-313). This makes the system robust to incomplete caches.

  Bugs

  1. apply_converged_toggles_to_trade_log silently skips new toggles (Codex review bug #1). Line 227: if toggle not in FILTER_REGISTRY:
  continue. Any toggle that the diagnosis loop discovers and locks but which doesn't exist in FILTER_REGISTRY is silently skipped when
  applying to the Phase Z trade log. The Codex review flagged this. The col_map dict at lines 231-252 is the actual filter implementation — it
   should be checked instead of (or in addition to) FILTER_REGISTRY.

  2. apply_converged_toggles_to_trade_log col_map is stale. The col_map is a duplicate of filter logic that also exists in _pre_filter_signals
   and _bad_mask. Three separate implementations of the same toggle semantics. If a new toggle is added to the diagnosis matrix, it needs to
  be added in three places: _DIMENSIONS in matrix.py, _bad_mask in matrix.py, and col_map in loop.py. Divergence is inevitable.

  3. build_strategy_card_from_state uses wrong final_pf. Line 197: state.hypothesis_log[-1].real_pf — this is the real_pf of the LAST
  hypothesis entry, which could be a LOST hypothesis from the final round. The correct final_pf should be the real_pf of the last LOCKED
  hypothesis, or the baseline_pf if nothing was locked. If the last round converged with all 3 hypotheses below threshold, the last entry
  would be a LOST with a PF lower than the actual converged baseline.

  4. _bad_mask for bollinger_upper_rising only handles longs. Line 114: return (s != True) & (d == "long"). This means short-side bollinger
  expansion is never flagged as "bad" — it always returns False for shorts. For shorts, bollinger_lower_falling should be checked instead. The
   diagnosis matrix will undercount the short-side bollinger leak.

  5. _bad_mask for bollinger_bandwidth_crossover_up has the same short-side issue. Line 116 handles both directions but uses
  bollinger_bandwidth_crossover_down for shorts. However, the dimension spec only declares bollinger_bandwidth_crossover_up as the column
  (line 51 of matrix.py). If the trade log doesn't have bollinger_bandwidth_crossover_down, the trade_log.get() fallback returns all-False,
  making shorts immune to this filter.

  6. Winner toggle not locked when pf_improvement < threshold. Lines 155-168 in loop.py: if the best hypothesis improves PF by 0.04 (below
  0.05 threshold), the toggle is NOT locked but the consecutive_low_impact_rounds counter increments. However, the winner's real_pf is still
  used as the new baseline_pf only when locked (line 157). This means if 3 consecutive rounds each improve PF by 0.04, the cumulative
  improvement is 0.12 but none of the toggles get locked. The convergence logic misses gradual improvements.

  Actually, re-reading more carefully: line 157 baseline_pf = winner_pf is inside the if pf_improvement >= threshold block. So in the <
  threshold case, baseline_pf stays the same. The next round re-diagnoses against the same baseline. This is correct — the toggle is not
  locked, so the baseline shouldn't change. Not a bug, just a design choice to only lock discrete jumps.

  7. Diagnosis runs on the same trade log every round. Line 85: trade_log = load_trade_log(base_dir, state.strategy_key) is called once
  outside the loop. Each round re-diagnoses this same trade log. But locked toggles are not applied to the trade log — the diagnosis always
  sees the full Phase 0 population. This means the ranked table doesn't change between rounds (same trades, same dimensions). The only thing
  that changes is the prompt (which includes prior round results). The LLM is expected to pick different toggles based on prior lessons, but
  the diagnosis data it sees is identical.

  This is a significant design issue. The production hypothesis pipeline tells Opus "here are the ranked dimensions" but those rankings never
  update as toggles get locked. Opus must infer which dimensions are now irrelevant based on prior rounds. This is workable but fragile — it
  depends entirely on the LLM's ability to track state across rounds.

  ---
  Design concerns

  8. backtest_factory.py is 800+ lines and growing. The _pre_filter_signals function alone is ~500 lines — a massive switch statement over
  gate keys. Each gate has its own alignment, normalization, and directional logic. Adding a new gate requires ~20 lines of boilerplate. This
  violates the 800-line file limit from your coding standards.

  9. _pre_filter_signals and _bad_mask encode the same toggle semantics differently. _bad_mask operates on trade-log columns (post-hoc,
  row-level). _pre_filter_signals operates on signal DataFrames (pre-backtest, date × symbol matrices). They must produce equivalent results
  but use completely different code paths. There's no shared abstraction — if you add a new toggle, you implement the same logic twice in two
  different representations.

  10. The exit resimulator's _trade_bricks lookup is fragile. Line 50-53: it tries index-based slicing bricks.loc[entry_date:exit_date], which
   depends on the brick index being a proper DatetimeIndex sorted chronologically. If bricks have duplicate timestamps or the 05:00 vs 00:00
  index mismatch, the slice may return empty or wrong rows. No tolerance or validation.

  11. _swing_breakout_trail is a no-op. Line 68: it returns the original PnL unchanged. This means the "swing_breakout_trail" exit method in
  the resimulation always produces PF delta = 0. It's included to establish a baseline comparison point, which is fine semantically, but it's
  named as if it does something and runs in the thread pool unnecessarily.

  Summary

  The production hypothesis pipeline is architecturally sound — clean data contracts, principled convergence, direction-aware diagnosis,
  cross-strategy learning, proper LLM fallback. The code quality is generally high with consistent immutability patterns.

  The most significant issues are:

  1. Diagnosis doesn't re-slice after locking toggles — the LLM sees the same ranked table every round and must track state from prior results
   alone
  2. Triple implementation of toggle semantics — _bad_mask, _pre_filter_signals, and apply_converged_toggles_to_trade_log must stay in sync
  manually
  3. apply_converged_toggles_to_trade_log skips toggles not in FILTER_REGISTRY — Phase Z may evaluate a less-filtered trade set than intended
  4. Short-side bollinger diagnosis is incomplete — _bad_mask only handles longs for bollinger expansion
  5. backtest_factory.py at 800+ lines needs extraction of the gate dispatch into a registry-driven pattern

  Step 3: Diagnose failure at the pattern level
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | What we ask                                                   |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Among actual baseline trades, what structural failures        |
  | separate better vs worse trades?                              |
  |                                                              |
  | Current structural families we already found:                 |

  | - orderly correction                                          |

  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  Step 4: Build a structural mechanism rule
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | What this means                                               |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Convert the failure story into a real-engine rule, e.g.       |
  | - enough runway before setup                                  |
  | - pullback depth is meaningful                                |
  | - correction is orderly                                       |
  | - breakout is still fresh / not too mature                    |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  Step 5: Confirm the mechanism in the real engine
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | What we do                                                   |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Run the mechanism as a real-engine strategy variant,         |
  | not as a proxy mask only.                                    |
  |                                                              |
  | Current leader:                                              |
  | - fresh_breakout_maturity_real_engine                        |
  | - PF 1.4962 vs baseline 1.2898                               |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  Step 6: Add book-based qualifiers around the mechanism
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Important rule                                                |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Filters are not tested as random global toggles.              |
  | They are tested as qualifiers on top of a chosen mechanism.   |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  Step 7: Keep stock selection separate from pattern qualifiers
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Stock selection layer                                         |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | - stock_rs_filter                                              |
  | - sector_rs_filter                                             |
  | - mtf_score_min                                                |
  | - breadth_gate                                                 |
  |                                                              |

  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  | - ema_dual_alignment                                           |
  | - donchian_zone_alignment                                      |
  | - donchian_direction_alignment                                 |
  |                                                              |
  | Momentum qualifiers                                            |
  | - macd_signal_alignment                                        |
  | - macd_near_zero_avoid                                         |
  | - macd_divergence_avoid                                        |
  | - rsi_midline_support                                          |
  | - rsi_divergence_avoid                                         |
  | - rsi_trendline_alignment                                      |
  | - brick_zone_weakening_warning                                 |
  | - brick_zone_divergence_avoid                                  |
  | - brick_indicator_confirmation                                 |
  |                                                              |
  | Volatility qualifiers                                          |
  | - bollinger_expansion_alignment                                |
  | - bollinger_bandwidth_confirmation                             |
  |                                                              |
  | Risk / extension                                               |
  | - five_brick_risk                                              |
  | - prior_ext_negated_filter                                     |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  Step 9: Test one qualifier family at a time
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Why                                                           |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | So we know whether the edge comes from:                       |
  | - the mechanism itself                                        |
  | - stock selection context                                     |
  | - trend confirmation                                          |
  | - momentum confirmation                                       |
  | - volatility/risk context                                     |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  Step 10: Keep a support floor
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Current discipline                                            |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Do not trust filters/mechanisms that improve PF only by       |
  | collapsing the sample too hard.                               |
  | We are using support-aware diagnosis and generally want       |
  | credible kept-trade counts, around 300+ when possible.        |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  Step 11: Promote only real-engine winners
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Promotion rule                                                |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | A mechanism or qualifier is carried forward only if the       |
  | real engine confirms it, not just the diagnosis proxy table.  |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  Step 12: Then move to validation / MC / OOS
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | After mechanism + qualifier survive real engine               |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  | - Monte Carlo / robustness                                     |
  | - OOS / temporal validation                                    |
  | - later ranking across mechanism families                      |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+

  Short version:

  Baseline -> enrich with book-based context -> diagnose structural failure ->
  build mechanism -> confirm in real engine -> add stock selection and
  indicator qualifiers one family at a time -> keep support floor ->
  promote only real-engine survivors

  That is the current mechanism path after the book-based filter rewrite and the stock-selection / cache issues were fixed.

Hypothesis Pipeline Performance Review

  What's already well-optimized

  1. Factory caches aggressively. backtest_factory.py has three cache layers:
  - _cache_store (line 193): load_caches_for_key called once per StrategyKey, reused across all rounds
  - _base_signal_store (line 195): generate_renko_signals + execution OHLCV + entry trigger signals computed once per key with thread-safe
  double-checked locking (lines 208-316)
  - _execution_ohlcv_store (line 194): 5-minute OHLCV loaded once per (timeframe, symbol set), shared across keys

  This means the 3 parallel hypothesis backtests per round do NOT reload caches or regenerate signals. They only differ in which gates are
  applied. This is correct.

  2. Hypothesis backtests are parallel. runner.py:110: ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) runs all 3 hypotheses concurrently. Each gets
  current_toggles + [new_toggle] and runs through the factory's backtest_fn, which benefits from the cached base signals.

  3. Exit resimulation is parallel. exit_resimulator.py:234: ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=6) runs up to 6 exit methods concurrently.

  4. Phase 0 sweep is checkpoint-driven. phase0_runner.py:278-284: already-completed keys skip entirely.

  5. Cross-strategy learning is inherently sequential. pipeline.py:233: strategies run one at a time because later strategies need completed
  strategy cards from earlier ones. This is a design constraint, not a performance bug.

  ---
  Performance issues

  1. Diagnosis matrix recomputes PF 22+ times per round.
  matrix.py:145-161: for each of 22 dimensions, _bad_mask filters the trade log, then _pf(_pnl_series(trade_log[~mask])) recomputes PF on the
  filtered subset. Each PF computation iterates the full PnL series.

  The baseline PnL series and total loss are computed once (lines 141-142), but each dimension's proxy PF creates a new filtered view and sums
   wins/losses independently.

  With ~1400 trades × 22 dimensions × up to 20 rounds = ~616K PF computations total. Each is O(N) on the trade log. Not huge individually, but
   in aggregate it adds up — especially since each round re-runs the full 22-dimension scan.

  Impact: Low-medium. The trade log is small (~1400 rows), so each PF is microseconds. Aggregate: ~1-2 seconds per round, ~20-40 seconds total
   across 20 rounds. Acceptable.

  2. _current_trade_log can trigger a full re-backtest + enrichment per round.
  loop.py:106-134: if the saved trade log's source_toggles don't match the current locked_toggles, it calls _persist_current_trade_log (line
  123) which runs the full backtest via backtest_fn(toggles) + trade log enrichment (indicators, breadth, RS, etc.).

  This happens every time a toggle is locked — the trade log must be refreshed with the new filter applied. The factory caches base signals
  but the enrichment step (enrich_trade_log at line 87) recomputes all Layer 1-4 metadata for every trade. With ~1400 trades and 30+ indicator
   lookups per trade, this is ~42K asof-lookups per round.

  Impact: Medium. Enrichment is I/O-light (indicator cache is in memory) but CPU-bound due to per-trade iteration. ~5-10 seconds per round
  after a toggle lock. With ~5-8 locking rounds: ~40-80 seconds total.

  3. Trade log is re-loaded from parquet at the start of each round.
  loop.py:172: _current_trade_log(state, base_dir, backtest_fn) calls load_trade_log(base_dir, state.strategy_key) which reads parquet from
  disk (line 111). If source_toggles match, it returns immediately. But if not, it writes the refreshed log to disk, then on the next round,
  re-reads it. This is a disk round-trip per round.

  Impact: Low. Parquet read of ~1400 rows is milliseconds.

  4. Phase 0 sweep is sequential across keys.
  phase0_runner.py:291: for k in pending: ... runs each strategy key one at a time. The comment explains why: "Signal generation and backtest
  run in the main thread so detector-backed signal composition stays consistent." The backtest loop within each key uses ThreadPoolExecutor,
  but keys themselves are sequential.

  With ALL_STRATEGY_KEYS = strategies × brick sizes (e.g., 10 strategies × 3 bricks = 30 keys), this means 30 sequential Phase 0 runs. Each
  involves loading caches, generating signals, and running the backtest.

  Impact: High for the Phase 0 stage specifically. On 8 CPUs, only 1 is used for signal generation; ThreadPoolExecutor provides some
  parallelism within the backtest loop but the signal generation per key is single-threaded.

  5. pipeline.py:233 runs diagnosis sequentially across survivor strategies.
  Intentional for cross-strategy learning, but on 8 CPUs, this means only 1 CPU is active during diagnosis. The 3-hypothesis parallel backtest
   (ThreadPoolExecutor with 3 workers) uses at most 3 CPUs, leaving 5 idle.

  Impact: Medium. If there are 5 survivors each needing 8 rounds × (LLM call + 3 backtests), total wall time is dominated by LLM latency +
  sequential rounds.

  6. LLM call is the blocking bottleneck per round.
  loop.py:199-213: Opus call (or Codex fallback) is synchronous. Typical latency: 5-15 seconds per call. With 5-8 rounds per strategy × 5
  strategies = 25-40 LLM calls. At 10 seconds each: 4-7 minutes just waiting for LLM responses.

  This is inherently serial — you can't parallelize LLM calls across rounds because each round depends on the prior round's results. But you
  could overlap LLM calls across independent strategies (if cross-strategy learning weren't required for all of them).

  Impact: High. LLM latency likely dominates diagnosis time.

  7. Continuous summary and exit resimulation are not computed.
  matrix.py:181-191: compute_diagnosis_matrix computes continuous summary inline. But exit_resim_results defaults to an empty tuple (line 163)
   — the resimulator is never called during the diagnosis loop. The exit resim results shown in the Opus prompt come from... nowhere in the
  current loop code.

  Checking loop.py — there's no call to resimulate_exit_methods. The diagnosis object's exit_resim_results is always empty. The prompt at
  prompt.py:47-51 formats it but it's always empty.

  Impact: Not a performance issue — it's a missing feature. The exit resimulator is wired and parallel but never invoked. If you want exit
  resim data in the Opus prompt, you'd need to call it in the loop after compute_diagnosis_matrix.

  - _cache_store (line 193): load_caches_for_key called once per StrategyKey, reused across all rounds
  - _base_signal_store (line 195): generate_renko_signals + execution OHLCV + entry trigger signals computed once per key with thread-safe
  double-checked locking (lines 208-316)
  - _execution_ohlcv_store (line 194): 5-minute OHLCV loaded once per (timeframe, symbol set), shared across keys

  This means the 3 parallel hypothesis backtests per round do NOT reload caches or regenerate signals. They only differ in which gates are
  applied. This is correct.

  2. Hypothesis backtests are parallel. runner.py:110: ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) runs all 3 hypotheses concurrently. Each gets
  current_toggles + [new_toggle] and runs through the factory's backtest_fn, which benefits from the cached base signals.

  3. Exit resimulation is parallel. exit_resimulator.py:234: ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=6) runs up to 6 exit methods concurrently.

  4. Phase 0 sweep is checkpoint-driven. phase0_runner.py:278-284: already-completed keys skip entirely.

  5. Cross-strategy learning is inherently sequential. pipeline.py:233: strategies run one at a time because later strategies need completed
  strategy cards from earlier ones. This is a design constraint, not a performance bug.

  ---
  Performance issues

  1. Diagnosis matrix recomputes PF 22+ times per round.
  matrix.py:145-161: for each of 22 dimensions, _bad_mask filters the trade log, then _pf(_pnl_series(trade_log[~mask])) recomputes PF on the
  filtered subset. Each PF computation iterates the full PnL series.

  The baseline PnL series and total loss are computed once (lines 141-142), but each dimension's proxy PF creates a new filtered view and sums
   wins/losses independently.

  With ~1400 trades × 22 dimensions × up to 20 rounds = ~616K PF computations total. Each is O(N) on the trade log. Not huge individually, but
   in aggregate it adds up — especially since each round re-runs the full 22-dimension scan.

  Impact: Low-medium. The trade log is small (~1400 rows), so each PF is microseconds. Aggregate: ~1-2 seconds per round, ~20-40 seconds total
   across 20 rounds. Acceptable.

  2. _current_trade_log can trigger a full re-backtest + enrichment per round.
  loop.py:106-134: if the saved trade log's source_toggles don't match the current locked_toggles, it calls _persist_current_trade_log (line
  123) which runs the full backtest via backtest_fn(toggles) + trade log enrichment (indicators, breadth, RS, etc.).

  This happens every time a toggle is locked — the trade log must be refreshed with the new filter applied. The factory caches base signals
  but the enrichment step (enrich_trade_log at line 87) recomputes all Layer 1-4 metadata for every trade. With ~1400 trades and 30+ indicator
   lookups per trade, this is ~42K asof-lookups per round.

  Impact: Medium. Enrichment is I/O-light (indicator cache is in memory) but CPU-bound due to per-trade iteration. ~5-10 seconds per round
  after a toggle lock. With ~5-8 locking rounds: ~40-80 seconds total.

  3. Trade log is re-loaded from parquet at the start of each round.
  loop.py:172: _current_trade_log(state, base_dir, backtest_fn) calls load_trade_log(base_dir, state.strategy_key) which reads parquet from
  disk (line 111). If source_toggles match, it returns immediately. But if not, it writes the refreshed log to disk, then on the next round,
  re-reads it. This is a disk round-trip per round.

  Impact: Low. Parquet read of ~1400 rows is milliseconds.

  4. Phase 0 sweep is sequential across keys.
  phase0_runner.py:291: for k in pending: ... runs each strategy key one at a time. The comment explains why: "Signal generation and backtest
  run in the main thread so detector-backed signal composition stays consistent." The backtest loop within each key uses ThreadPoolExecutor,
  but keys themselves are sequential.

  With ALL_STRATEGY_KEYS = strategies × brick sizes (e.g., 10 strategies × 3 bricks = 30 keys), this means 30 sequential Phase 0 runs. Each
  involves loading caches, generating signals, and running the backtest.

  Impact: High for the Phase 0 stage specifically. On 8 CPUs, only 1 is used for signal generation; ThreadPoolExecutor provides some
  parallelism within the backtest loop but the signal generation per key is single-threaded.

  5. pipeline.py:233 runs diagnosis sequentially across survivor strategies.
  Intentional for cross-strategy learning, but on 8 CPUs, this means only 1 CPU is active during diagnosis. The 3-hypothesis parallel backtest
   (ThreadPoolExecutor with 3 workers) uses at most 3 CPUs, leaving 5 idle.

  Impact: Medium. If there are 5 survivors each needing 8 rounds × (LLM call + 3 backtests), total wall time is dominated by LLM latency +
  sequential rounds.

  6. LLM call is the blocking bottleneck per round.
  loop.py:199-213: Opus call (or Codex fallback) is synchronous. Typical latency: 5-15 seconds per call. With 5-8 rounds per strategy × 5
  strategies = 25-40 LLM calls. At 10 seconds each: 4-7 minutes just waiting for LLM responses.

  This is inherently serial — you can't parallelize LLM calls across rounds because each round depends on the prior round's results. But you
  could overlap LLM calls across independent strategies (if cross-strategy learning weren't required for all of them).

  Impact: High. LLM latency likely dominates diagnosis time.

  7. Continuous summary and exit resimulation are not computed.
  matrix.py:181-191: compute_diagnosis_matrix computes continuous summary inline. But exit_resim_results defaults to an empty tuple (line 163)
   — the resimulator is never called during the diagnosis loop. The exit resim results shown in the Opus prompt come from... nowhere in the
  current loop code.

  Checking loop.py — there's no call to resimulate_exit_methods. The diagnosis object's exit_resim_results is always empty. The prompt at
  prompt.py:47-51 formats it but it's always empty.

  Impact: Not a performance issue — it's a missing feature. The exit resimulator is wired and parallel but never invoked. If you want exit
  resim data in the Opus prompt, you'd need to call it in the loop after compute_diagnosis_matrix.

  3. The toggles and what they filter (from ec2_diagnosis_compute.py lines 61-152):

  | Toggle                           | What it filters                                 | Book field used

  |----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|--------------------
  -------------------------------|

  != -1                          |

   != -1                         |

                                 |
  | breadth_gate                     | Remove trades in euphoria breadth zone          | sector_breadth_zone
   != "euphoria"                 |

  matches trade direction        |

  matches direction               |

  matches direction                   |

  donchian_direction_alignment == True              |
  | macd_signal_alignment            | Require MACD aligned with direction             | macd_signal_state
  matches direction               |
  | macd_near_zero_avoid             | Remove trades with MACD near zero               | macd_near_zero !=
  True                            |
  | macd_divergence_avoid            | Remove trades with bearish MACD divergence      |
  macd_bearish_divergence != True                   |
  | rsi_midline_support              | Require RSI above 50 for longs                  | rsi_midline_state
  matches direction               |
  | rsi_divergence_avoid             | Remove trades with bearish RSI divergence       |
  rsi_bearish_divergence != True                    |
  | rsi_trendline_alignment          | Require RSI trendline matches direction         |
  rsi_trendline_up/down matches direction           |
  | brick_zone_weakening_warning     | Remove trades where brick zone is weakening     |
  brick_zone_weakening != True                      |
  | brick_zone_divergence_avoid      | Remove trades with brick zone divergence        |
  brick_zone_bearish_divergence != True             |
  | brick_indicator_confirmation     | Require brick indicator matches direction       |
  brick_indicator_bullish/bearish matches direction |
  | bollinger_expansion_alignment    | Require Bollinger band expanding with direction |
  bollinger_upper_rising/lower_falling              |
  | bollinger_bandwidth_confirmation | Require bandwidth crossover matches direction   |
  bollinger_bandwidth_crossover_up/down             |

  stop_distance_bricks <= 5                         |

  Stage 5 — Evaluate (parallel, no LLM)

  Two evaluators run simultaneously:

  scripts/sidecar2/evaluate_mechanism_manifest_v2.py → mechanism_manifest_eval_v2.json
  - Loads enriched trade log
  - For each test in the manifest:
    - Applies the conditions as a filter against the trade log DataFrame
    - Computes: PF with filter, PF without, PF impact, kept/removed counts, win rate change
  - Fast — pure pandas filtering, no backtest engine. ~1-5 min.

  scripts/sidecar2/evaluate_mechanism_real_engine_v2.py → mechanism_real_engine_eval_v2.json
  - For each test in the manifest:
    - Loads renko signals + OHLCV from cache
    - Applies the candidate rule as a toggle gate via apply_trade_log_toggles() from toggle_semantics.py
    - Runs the actual run_renko_backtest() — full simulation, same engine as production
    - Produces real PF, real trade count, real win rate
  - Slow — full backtest per candidate. ~10-30 min.

  Why both? The replay evaluator is fast but approximate — it filters existing trades. The real engine
  re-runs the entire backtest with the filter active, which can produce different results because entry
  timing and position management change.

⛬  Yes

   The current notes are often too extraction-led and not synthesis-led, so for many sites they’re not very useful.

   What’s happening

   Right now the pipeline mostly:
   •  fetches page text
   •  extracts visible content
   •  dumps that into markdown with metadata

   That works for articles, but not for site understanding.

   Why ecommerce/SaaS notes feel bad

   For a store, a useful note should summarize:
   •  what kind of business it is
   •  product categories
   •  brand/style positioning
   •  online vs offline presence
   •  store locations if present
   •  price band / geography / contact signals

   For SaaS, it should summarize:
   •  what the product does
   •  target users
   •  key features / use cases
   •  pricing / demo / trial signals
   •  integrations / enterprise vs self-serve

   The current extractor does not reliably infer or structure that.

   So yes

   Without that higher-level summarization/classification layer, many notes are only partially useful and sometimes nearly useless.

   What to do

   The fix is not just config tuning.
   You need a post-extraction enrichment step that:
   •  classifies site type (ecommerce, saas, media, directory, etc.)
   •  extracts structured fields by type
   •  writes a synthesized summary instead of raw page fragments

   If you want, I can design and implement that enrichment layer in this repo.

Issue

  Pipeline launched without RELEASE_BUNDLE_URI. The auto-build path tried to build + upload a release inline. The S3 upload failed silently. The pipeline exited with status=unknown. 30+ minutes wasted
  before switching to the already-uploaded bundle.

  Root Cause

  My D1 fix ("auto-build release when no URI provided") coupled two operations that have different reliability profiles into a single critical path:

  - Build (local disk, deterministic, fast) — always works
  - S3 upload (network-dependent, auth-dependent, region-dependent) — can fail

  By putting the upload inline in run_pipeline_local.sh, I created a new failure mode that didn't exist before. Previously the pipeline either had an explicit URI (verified upfront) or cloned from git
  (also reliable). My "convenience" path introduced the least reliable option (just-in-time S3 upload) as the default.

  How I fixed it

  Separated the two concerns into distinct operations:

  1. scripts/publish_release.sh — standalone script that builds, uploads, verifies, and prints the URI. Run this BEFORE the pipeline. If it fails, you know immediately and can fix it (re-auth, fix
  network) before committing to an EC2 launch.
  2. run_pipeline_local.sh — now requires RELEASE_BUNDLE_URI. Verifies it exists in S3 before doing anything. Fails with a clear message pointing to publish_release.sh if missing.

  Why this is the ideal solution

  Separation of failure domains. Publishing (network I/O to S3) and launching (EC2 instance + SSM commands) are independent operations with different failure modes. Coupling them means a network blip
  during upload kills the entire pipeline. Separating them means:
  - Publish can fail and retry without wasting EC2 time
  - Pipeline launch knows the artifact exists before committing resources
  - No silent failure — each step has explicit success/failure output

  No hidden automation. The auto-build was "magic" that hid what was happening. The two-step workflow is explicit: you publish, you see it succeed, you launch. No surprises.

  Matches how production releases work. Build artifacts are published once, then referenced by URI. They're not built just-in-time during deployment. This is the same principle.

Issue

  Redeploying code on a reused EC2 instance destroyed the runtime cache. Sidecar2 failed immediately: CACHE_DIR=/opt/autoresearch/cache didn't exist.

  Root Cause

  Architectural coupling: Mutable runtime state (cache) and immutable release code shared the same root directory /opt/autoresearch. The bootstrap's rm -rf /opt/autoresearch (line 50) is designed to
  clean-install the release, but it also destroys the cache. The subsequent S3 sync is supposed to restore it, but it's fragile — if it fails partially, or if the pipeline moves faster than the sync,
  downstream stages find no cache.

  This isn't a one-off bug. It's a design flaw: code is immutable and should be replaceable without affecting state. State is mutable and should persist across deploys. Putting both under the same rm
  -rf target violates that separation.

  Fix

  - Cache moved to /var/lib/autoresearch/cache (persists across rm -rf /opt/autoresearch)
  - Data moved to /var/lib/autoresearch/data
  - Bootstrap creates symlinks: /opt/autoresearch/cache → /var/lib/autoresearch/cache so relative-path code still works
  - 40 files updated: all hardcoded defaults changed, all scripts read CACHE_DIR from env
  - Bootstrap explicitly passes CACHE_DIR and DATA_DIR in reuse-mode SSM command

  Why this is the ideal fix

  The release directory is now purely immutable — rm -rf /opt/autoresearch only destroys code, which is immediately replaced by the new release. Cache data survives because it's on a separate path. No
  re-download needed on redeploy. The symlink provides backward compatibility without coupling the lifecycles. do you agree

The pipeline had three independently invented observability systems that used different schemas, different file formats, different stage names, and provided different subsets of visibility. During
  live runs, operators couldn't answer basic questions — where is the run, what is it doing, is it alive, how long is each step taking — without SSH-ing into the EC2 instance and reading ad-hoc logs.

  The three old systems:
  1. write_stage() in phase0_artifacts.py — snapshot phase0_status.json, used by Phase 0 + diagnosis
  2. write_progress() + sync_progress() in run_mechanism_sidecar2_ec2.sh — snapshot sidecar2_progress.json, used by sidecar2 shell
  3. append_audit() + sync_time_audit() in same file — append-only sidecar2_time_audit.json, timing only
  4. _write_progress() in run_mechanism_sidecar2.py — yet another variant for sidecar2 Python
  5. DiagnosisProgress class in ec2_diagnosis_compute.py — wrapper around write_stage with a heartbeat thread

  Live run evidence: sidecar2 was clearly active with many prompt/response turns, yet S3 progress.json stayed stale and time_audit.json stayed at "preflight." The operator was blind.

  Analysis

  Root cause was architectural fragmentation:
  - Different schemas: System 1 used {stage, updated_at}, System 2 used {status, current_stage, updated_at_utc}, System 3 used {name, returncode, elapsed_seconds}
  - Different writers: 5 separate implementations, no shared code
  - Different output models: Systems 1+2 overwrite (snapshot), System 3 appends. No system does both.
  - No heartbeats in sidecar2: Diagnosis had heartbeat, sidecar2 didn't — so sidecar2 went dark between stage boundaries
  - No timing in Phase 0/diagnosis: Only sidecar2 had time_audit.json
  - S3 sync only on started/completed/failed: Progress and heartbeat events weren't synced, so S3 stayed stale during long stages
  - Stage names ad-hoc: No canonical taxonomy, each component invented its own names

  1. Unified event framework (3 new files)

  src/backtesting/observability/writer.py — PipelineEventWriter class:
  - Thread-safe, append-only event emitter
  - Writes events.jsonl (one JSON line per event — primary debug source)
  - Derives progress.json (latest state snapshot) and time_audit.json (per-stage durations) from the event stream
  - Built-in heartbeat thread (configurable interval, default 30s)
  - S3 sync on EVERY event type (not just started/completed)
  - Syncs all 3 files: events.jsonl, progress.json, time_audit.json
  - PIPELINE_OBSERVABILITY=off disables all writes (zero overhead)

  src/backtesting/observability/stages.py — 85 canonical stage names covering:
  - pipeline.* — local orchestrator (17 stages)
  - bootstrap.* — EC2 bootstrap (10 stages)
  - phase0.* — Phase 0 (9 stages)
  - diagnosis.* — diagnosis (16 stages)
  - sidecar2.* — sidecar2 (12 stages)
  - hypothesis.* — hypothesis loop (5 stages)
  - watcher.* — local watchers (3 stages)
  - cache_build.* — cache building (6 stages)

  scripts/pipeline_events.sh — Bash helper that delegates ALL logic to the Python writer via a one-liner. Full feature parity: substage, counters, heartbeats, S3 sync. No duplicated derive logic.

  2. Stage name enforcement

  scripts/lint_stage_names.py — scans all .py and .sh files, verifies every emitted stage name exists in stages.py. 85 canonical names, 0 drift. Catches drift before it reaches production.

  - Removed write_stage(), stage_path(), STAGE_FILE from phase0_artifacts.py

  - Removed write_progress(), sync_progress(), append_audit(), sync_time_audit(), init_audit(), collect_artifacts() from run_mechanism_sidecar2_ec2.sh

Claims 1 & 2 (startup _wevent not guarded): NOT VALID bugs.
  _wevent() itself has type pipeline_event &>/dev/null && pipeline_event ... || true. The || true covers the entire command chain. If pipeline_event doesn't exist or fails, || true catches it. The
  caller _wevent started watcher.polling ... doesn't need its own || true because the function is already fail-open internally. This is safe.

  Claims 3 & 4 (bootstrap/launch inline not isolated): NOT VALID bugs.
  _event() has type pipeline_event &>/dev/null && pipeline_event ... || true — fail-open. _levent() has the same. The calls are inline in the control flow but the function itself is fail-open.
  Structurally less clean than sidecar2's dedicated helper, but functionally safe — instrumentation cannot crash the business path.

  Claims 5 & 6 (hypothesis/renko watchers mix instrumentation): PARTIALLY VALID.
  The _wevent calls in the business loop ARE already guarded with 2>/dev/null || true at the call site (lines 135, 145, 127, 128, 131). So they're functionally safe. But the _wevent started
  watcher.polling at line 106 (hypothesis) and line 70 (renko) are NOT guarded at the call site — they rely on _wevent()'s internal guard. This is safe because _wevent is fail-open, but it's
  inconsistent style.

  Verdict: Zero actual bugs. All 6 items are already functionally fail-open. The inconsistency is stylistic (some callers add 2>/dev/null || true redundantly, some don't), not a correctness issue. The
  _wevent/_event/_levent functions are ALL fail-open internally via || true.

  The audit's framing ("not wrapped with || true") is checking the caller, but the safety guarantee is in the function definition. Both are valid patterns — defense at the function level vs defense at
  the call site. We use function-level defense consistently.

Issue: macOS mktemp only substitutes Xs when they're the trailing characters in the template. mktemp /tmp/s2w_prompt_XXXXXX.txt treats XXXXXX as literal because .txt follows them. The file is always
  /tmp/s2w_prompt_XXXXXX.txt — deterministic, not random. Second call fails with "File exists."

  Analysis: The mktemp man page on macOS says the template must end with X characters. Anything after the Xs is not part of the substitution. Linux mktemp has --suffix but macOS doesn't.

  Fix: mktemp with trailing Xs (creates randomized file), then mv to add .txt extension. This is cross-platform, keeps the file type hint, and guarantees unique names.

  Why it's the right fix: It solves all three requirements — randomized (unique per call), has .txt extension (file type visible), works on both macOS and Linux. No shortcut (dropping the extension) or
  hack (appending to variable without renaming the actual file).

Your analysis is correct on the core problem but misses a second bug in the same function, and I'd refine one point of the proposed fix.

  What I verified independently

  1. The math checks out. _bool_series converts NA→False. With 1349 NA + 3 False + 0 True for crossover_up, the keep mask (up & long) is all-False. Diagnosis correctly
  reports kept=0, removed=1352. The computation is right; the inputs are semantically wrong.

  2. The root cause is two bugs, not one.

  Bug A (the one you identified): Event sparsity. bollinger_bandwidth_crossover_up is a one-brick event — True only on the exact brick where bandwidth crosses above its
  MA. By definition, this rarely coincides with the trade entry brick. Using it as a keep/reject mask is structurally degenerate for diagnosis.

  Bug B (you didn't call out): The directional mapping contradicts Shah. The keep mask is (crossover_up & long) | (crossover_down & short). But Shah Ch 7 explicitly says:

  ▎ "A bandwidth crossover combined with a Renko pattern is a potent setup... crossover direction alone does not specify trade direction — use the pattern for direction"

  And from the signals catalog:

  ▎ "Bollinger Bandwidth crossover (either direction) — A bandwidth crossover combined with a Renko pattern is a potent setup; crossover direction alone does not specify
  trade direction"

  Shah says both crossover directions are valid for both trade directions. The code incorrectly maps up→long, down→short. Even if crossover_up weren't sparse, the
  directional split is wrong per the source material. The correct crossover keep mask would be crossover_up | crossover_down regardless of direction.

  3. bollinger_bandwidth_above_ma exists and is the right replacement for diagnosis. It's computed at renko_filter_states.py:468 as bb_bandwidth > bandwidth_ma — a
  persistent state, True whenever bandwidth is above its moving average. This directly captures Shah's "expansion vs consolidation" concept and will produce a
  non-degenerate partition across trades.

  4. The execution mask has the same bug. Line 525 uses _trendline_alignment_mask("bb_bandwidth_crossover_up", "bb_bandwidth_crossover_down"), which maps up→long gate,
  down→short gate. Per Shah, both crossover directions should pass for both trade directions.

  My refined fix proposal

  Fix 1: Diagnosis dimension — swap column to bollinger_bandwidth_above_ma

  In matrix.py:52, change the dimension from the sparse crossover event to the persistent state:

  # Before:
  _DimSpec("bollinger_bandwidth_crossover_up", "bollinger_bandwidth_crossover_up", "L2", "Volatility", "bollinger_bandwidth_confirmation"),

  # After:
  _DimSpec("bollinger_bandwidth_above_ma", "bollinger_bandwidth_above_ma", "L2", "Volatility", "bollinger_bandwidth_confirmation"),

  Fix 2: Keep mask — use above_ma instead of crossover events

  In toggle_semantics.py:491-495, _keep_bollinger_bandwidth should use the state, not the event:

  def _keep_bollinger_bandwidth(trade_log: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
      return _bool_series(trade_log, "bollinger_bandwidth_above_ma")

  No directional split needed — Shah says bandwidth is direction-neutral. Bandwidth above MA = expanding volatility = favorable for both long and short entries.

  Fix 3: Execution mask — same change

  In TOGGLE_SPECS line 525, the execution mask should use bb_bandwidth_above_ma instead of directional crossover columns:

  # Before:
  _trendline_alignment_mask("bb_bandwidth_crossover_up", "bb_bandwidth_crossover_down")

  # After:
  _derived_bool_mask("bb_bandwidth_above_ma", symmetric=True)

  symmetric=True means both long and short gates use the same condition, which matches Shah's "direction-neutral" semantics.

  Fix 4: Degeneracy guard in diagnosis matrix

  In matrix.py, before scoring a dimension, check for degenerate partitions:

  if kept_trades == 0 or removed_trades == 0:
      pf_impact, cap_saved = math.nan, 0.0  # mark as non-actionable

  This prevents any future sparse feature from producing misleading 100% capital_saved rows.

  What I disagree with (minor)

  You say "do not use sparse crossover-event features as hard diagnosis keep-masks." That's the right conclusion for diagnosis, but the crossover event itself is still a
  valid Shah signal — it's an entry timing signal ("pattern + crossover coincidence = potent setup"), not a regime filter. It should remain available as an enrichment
  column for sidecar2 discovery to examine, just not as a diagnosis keep/reject dimension.

⏺ Your proposal has the right instincts but I'd reorder the priorities and push back on one key point.

  Where I agree:

  - Feature typing metadata (your point 2) — highest leverage single change. Declaring dtype/semantic/density/direction per feature would have prevented the bollinger
  crossover-as-diagnosis-dimension bug, the float/int comparison bug, and the sparse-event-as-hard-filter class of issues. This is the foundation everything else builds

  - Pre-emission validation (your point 4) — second highest leverage. Computing matched trades before writing the manifest would have caught the scaffold_02 zero-trade
  failure immediately, without needing to run the full evaluation pipeline. The degeneracy guard we added to diagnosis is the same concept at a different layer.
  - Canonical comparators (your point 3) — already largely solved by the typed equality fix in _eval_condition. The remaining gap is manifest-side: the LLM emits -1 as an
  int, but the trade log stores -1.0 as float64. A schema-aware manifest writer could normalize values against the feature dtype metadata.

  Where I disagree:

  - Fixed rule template library (your point 1) — this over-constrains the LLM's creative value. The "hidden exhaustion" encoding (bollinger rising while bricks weaken) is
  a novel divergence concept that no template library would contain. The LLM's strength is proposing hypotheses humans wouldn't think of. The right approach is: let the
  LLM propose freely, validate rigorously before acceptance. Better compiler, not restricted source language.
  - Counterfactual explanation check (your point 6) — nice for debugging but doesn't prevent bad encodings. It's a reporting feature, not a gate.

  What I'd actually build, in priority order:

  1. Feature metadata in the catalog (dtype, semantic class, density, direction)
  2. Manifest builder validation that checks proposed conditions against the metadata — warn on sparse features in hard vetoes, type mismatches, unknown features
  3. Support-count pre-check before evaluation — reject rules that match 0 trades or produce degenerate partitions

  These three changes are small (maybe 80 lines total), don't constrain the LLM, and would have caught every bug we found in this session.

  Right now we have a strong forensic audit.
  To claim near-exhaustive coverage, you need a systematic completeness process, not more intuition.

  What “exhaustive” requires

  1. Define the exact scope
     You cannot prove “whole repo” loosely.
     You need a bounded claim like:

  - all code on the live Phase 0 -> diagnosis -> sidecar2 -> replay -> real-engine path
  - all artifact reuse paths touching that flow
  - all scripts callable by the production orchestrator for that flow

  Without a fixed scope, “exhaustive” is meaningless.

  2. Build the execution graph
     Enumerate every file/function actually reachable from:

  - run_pipeline_local.sh
  - EC2 bootstrap/launch scripts
  - Phase 0 runner
  - diagnosis compute
  - sidecar2 orchestrator
  - replay evaluator
  - real-engine evaluator
  - watcher/proxy path

  Then classify each node:

  - executed in production path
  - optional but callable
  - test-only
  - stale/legacy

  That gives you a closed set to audit.

  3. For each contract boundary, prove semantics match
     You need a contract table for:

  - Phase 0 artifact meaning
  - trade-log enrichment meaning
  - diagnosis dimension meaning
  - encoding/manifest meaning
  - replay meaning
  - real-engine meaning
  - promotion/rejection meaning

  Then verify for each field:

  - produced by whom
  - consumed by whom
  - same semantics or drift?

  This is how you catch the bugs we just found.

  4. Turn warnings into assertions
     You do not get exhaustiveness while the system silently degrades.

  Examples:

  - unsupported exact-rule conditions must error
  - stale artifact fingerprint mismatch must error
  - unknown manifest feature must error
  - replay-only candidate in real-engine must error
  - zero-support candidate must be quarantined, not scored normally

  Exhaustiveness requires fail-loud systems.

  5. Add invariant tests
     Not just example tests. Invariants.

  Examples:

  - every manifest exact_manifest_rule must either:
      - be fully supported in real-engine, or
      - be explicitly marked unsupported
  - every candidate’s replay semantics must match its rule_shape
  - every reused artifact must match fingerprint/version
  - every feature used in manifest must exist in feature catalog
  - every feature comparison must match feature dtype semantics

  These are the tests that turn audit findings into permanent guarantees.

  6. Add differential checks
     For a sample set of candidates, run:

  - replay exact semantics
  - real-engine exact semantics
  - compare expected direction of filtering / support counts / condition applicability

  Not PF equality, but semantic consistency.

  7. Force provenance into every persisted artifact
     Every artifact should carry:

  - source trade-log hash/fingerprint
  - code fingerprint
  - schema version
  - cache fingerprint
  - producing stage/run id

  Then reuse becomes mechanically verifiable.

  8. Do one final “closed-world” sweep
     Once the execution graph is fixed, grep every boundary keyword:

  - rule_shape
  - evaluation_scope
  - live_entry_safe
  - reuse_existing
  - trade_log
  - unsupported
  - warning
  - restore
  - fingerprint

  And verify each occurrence is either:

  - correct and necessary
  - dead
  - or needs patching

  That is how you get close to exhaustive.

  In practical terms
  If you want this level, the project needs:

  1. A formal audit scope
  5. Hard assertions instead of warnings
  6. Invariant test suite
  7. One final repo-wide closure pass

  You do not get “100% certainty” in a living repo.

• The ideal long-term solution is:

  One canonical rule contract, enforced end-to-end.

  Right now the system has too many places where meaning can drift:

  - discovery describes a mechanism
  - encoding writes a rule
  - manifest stores metadata
  - replay interprets it one way
  - real-engine interprets it another way
  - artifact reuse can carry old semantics forward

  The elegant fix is to make the pipeline compile and validate one shared rule model.

  What that looks like

  1. Canonical rule schema
     Every candidate should compile into one typed rule object with:

  - rule_shape
  - evaluation_mode
  - conditions
  - feature types
  - supported_in_replay
  - supported_in_real_engine
  - entry_safe
  - remove_matched vs keep_matched

  Not just freeform JSON fields.

  2. Single semantics engine
     Replay and real-engine should both consume the same semantic interpretation:

  - entry_veto means “remove matched trades/signals”
  - composite_filter means whatever the canonical schema says, once
  - no separate ad hoc interpretation in each evaluator

  So:

  - one compiler
  - one semantics definition
  - two execution backends

  3. Compile-time validation, not warning-time
     Before a candidate is accepted into the manifest:

  - verify all features exist
  - verify all condition values match feature types
  - verify the rule shape is compatible with feature semantics
  - verify replay/real-engine support
  - compute support counts on the enriched frame
  - reject degenerate or unsupported candidates

  If it fails, it should not enter the manifest as a normal candidate.

  4. Exact means exact
     If real-engine cannot faithfully evaluate a candidate:

  - do not run a weakened approximation and label it exact_manifest_rule
  - mark it:
      - unsupported_in_real_engine
      - or replay_only

  No silent degradation.

  5. Artifact provenance as part of the contract
     Every enriched trade log and derived artifact should carry:

  - code fingerprint
  - enrichment schema version
  - cache fingerprint
  - phase0 artifact fingerprint
  - source toggles
  2. No silent degradation
  3. Provenance-aware artifact reuse

  That is the long-term solution that closes the whole class of bugs, not just the examples we found.
